analysis.one_liner: Toughens federal child labor rules: bans minors from the most dangerous jobs, punishes supply-chain violators, and raises fines sharply.
analysis.headline: The CHILD Labor Act, which would have raised fines for employing children in dangerous jobs to up to $690,000 per violation, was introduced in October 2023 with 22 Democratic cosponsors and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the child labor provisions of the Fair Labor Standards Act. It would ban workers under 18 from manufacturing, mining, excavation, meat processing, demolition, and explosives; require the Labor Department to keep hazardous-occupation rules up to date; raise civil fines to up to $690,000 per violation and let children harmed on the job collect damages of at least $75,000 (or $750,000 for death or serious injury); make companies responsible for child labor used by their subcontractors; give the Labor Department power to issue stop-work orders and pursue corporate successors; and attach child-labor conditions to federal contracts and grants, with a three-year contracting ban for violators. It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Children who work, especially the teenagers and younger minors found in recent years on meatpacking kill floors, in roofing and demolition crews, and through staffing-agency subcontracting chains. The bill gives them a ban on the most dangerous jobs, an updated list of prohibited hazardous work, the right to collect substantial damages when harmed, and protection against retaliation for complaining. It also benefits law-abiding competitors, who would no longer be undercut by businesses cutting labor costs with illegal child labor, and it gives the Labor Department real enforcement tools — stop-work orders, supply-chain liability, and penalties that exceed the cost of doing business illegally.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Working children and teens in hazardous jobs

how_it_helps.text: It bans workers under 18 from a defined set of the most dangerous industries — manufacturing, mining, trenching or excavation, meat processing, demolition, and explosives — and requires the Labor Department to write and update rules naming other hazardous jobs and worksites.

It raises the stakes for violations: civil fines up to $151,380 per affected employee, or up to $690,000 per violation that causes a child's death or serious injury, both doubleable for repeat or willful violations.

It gives harmed children the right to sue for compensatory damages — at least $75,000 per affected employee, at least $750,000 for violations causing death or serious injury, and up to $1 million in punitive damages — with a 10-year window to bring the case.

It holds companies responsible for child labor anywhere in their supply chains: a firm can be liable for goods made by a subcontractor's illegal child labor unless it verified the chain and had no notice of a violation, and 'hot goods' shipped in violation can be barred from commerce for up to 180 days and tagged 'Unlawfully manufactured; child labor'.

It gives the Labor Department power to issue stop-work orders against violators — with affected workers paid at their regular rate for hours missed — and to hold corporate successors jointly liable so violators cannot escape fines by reorganizing under a new name.

It extends child-labor rules to federal contractors and grant recipients, including a three-year ban on new federal contracts for companies found in violation, and funds training programs to identify violations and support victims.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ or contract with minors — meat processors, manufacturers, mining and demolition contractors, staffing agencies, and federal contractors. They would face the under-18 ban in hazardous industries, supply-chain verification duties, much larger fines and damages for violations, stop-work orders that require paying idled workers, and a three-year federal contracting ban for violators. Indirectly, higher labor costs could be passed to consumers in affected supply chains.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers of minors and their subcontractors

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes significant compliance costs on employers of minors, including supply-chain recordkeeping, written assurances from every subcontractor, and labor-management committees on federal contracts — burdens that fall on compliant businesses trying to avoid liability for subcontractors' violations.

Penalties are severe: civil fines up to $690,000 per child-labor violation (doubleable), minimum $75,000 in damages per affected employee, and criminal fines up to $750,000 — levels opponents could argue exceed what most violations warrant, even though repeat, willful, and injury-causing violations are the main targets.

The bill requires the Labor Department to write many new rules within 180 days and re-determine hazardous-occupation rules, which would be a heavy regulatory lift and a target for legal and industry challenge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted: children doing dangerous work would gain real legal protections, real compensation when harmed, and an enforcer with tools to actually stop violations, and the bill already contains good-faith defenses for companies that verify their supply chains. The costs fall on businesses that hire minors, which would face steeper compliance work and much larger penalties for violations, including minimum $75,000 damages per affected child that some would call outsized for technical violations. On balance, the protections address a documented enforcement gap in industries where children have been injured and killed, and the design shows an effort to limit accidental liability. The main honest criticism is scope: it raises costs for all employers of minors to reach a small number of violators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, neither one ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the CHILD Labor Act on October 26, 2023, with 10 original cosponsors.
The same day, the House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Oversight and Accountability Committee — a routine split of jurisdiction between committees.
It ultimately drew 22 cosponsors, all House Democrats.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred; the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The companies that employ minors in hazardous work, including the meatpacking and staffing operations at the center of recent federal child-labor cases, are better off: fines stayed at the old low levels, supply-chain liability was never created, and no stop-work or contracting bans took effect. Children in dangerous jobs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers using child labor; fines stayed low

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — 22 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican — and the Republican-run committees and chamber never acted on it, so the bill died on party lines without a single recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill flatly bans workers under 18 from meat processing, an industry where federal investigators found children working overnight sanitation shifts in 2023. Its suppliers would face direct bans and their customers down the supply chain would share liability.

industries.industry: Manufacturers, mining, demolition and excavation contractors
industries.note: These industries would be barred from employing anyone under 18 in core operations and would face up to $690,000 fines per violation, doubleable. Companies would also be answerable for child labor at their subcontractors.

industries.industry: Federal contractors and grant recipients (construction and services)
industries.note: The bill attaches child-labor stipulations to Davis-Bacon and Service Contract Act work and federal assistance, adds compliance committees and training duties, allows contract cancellation, and imposes a three-year federal contracting ban on violators.

The bill targets the subcontracting chains that staffing intermediaries sit in: Labor Department investigators could demand records at any tier, secondary liability reaches every party in the chain, and successor-in-interest rules stop violators from reorganizing to escape liability.
